'''Chao-ting Wu''' ({{lang-zh|c=吳昭婷|p=Wú Zhāotíng}}; born January 24, 1954) is an American [[molecular biologist]]. After training at Harvard Medical School in genetics with [[William Martin Gelbart (geneticist)|William Gelbart]], at [[Stanford Medical School]] with [[David Hogness]], and in a fellowship at [[Massachusetts General Hospital]] in molecular biology, Wu began her independent academic career as an assistant professor in anatomy and cellular biology and then genetics at Harvard Medical School in 1993. After a period as a professor of pediatrics in the division of molecular medicine at the [[Boston Children's Hospital]], she returned to the Department of Genetics at Harvard Medical School as a full professor in 2007.

Wu's research has focused on the role of chromosome behavior gene activity and inheritance, with emphasis on widespread [[homology (biology)|homology]] effects, phenomena in which homology between chromosomes plays a role. Her studies have explored [[transvection (genetics)|transvection in genetics]], [[Polycomb-group proteins|polycomb-group genes]], chromatin pairing and [[chromatin remodeling|remodeling]], and the mechanisms of bridging [[promoter (genetics)|promoter]] and [[enhancer (genetics)|enhancer]] elements within and between chromosomes. She also studies [[ultra-conserved element]]s (UCEs), proposing that these highly conserved sequences play a role in maintaining genome integrity, and has discussed potential opportunities for therapeutics harnessing properties of UCEs in many venues, including in [[TEDx]] and the [[Google]]-sponsored [[Solve for X]] program.

Wu has made significant contributions in the area of science education in genetics, across many age groups, through work with the [[Smithsonian Institution]] and the [[National Museum of Natural History]] and is founding director of the [[Personal Genetics Education Project]], which works through schools, online curricula, teacher training, and producers and writers of the television and movie industry through involvement with the trade-supporting organization Hollywood, Health, & Society. She is daughter of author [[Nelson Ikon Wu]], sister of actor [[Ping Wu]], and colleague and spouse of Harvard and MIT scientist [[George M. Church]].

==Training and career==
Wu attended Mary Institute (now [[Mary Institute and St. Louis Country Day School]], MICDS) in [[St. Louis]], Missouri, from 1968 to 1972 and then completed her undergraduate BS degree in biology at [[Harvard University]]. She obtained her Ph.D. degree in 1984 from [[Harvard Medical School]] in Genetics and then following a brief period at [[Stanford Medical School]] with [[David Hogness]], set up a non-profit research institute in [[Cheshire, Connecticut]], called the Station for Natural Studies Inc., which received grant funding from the Whitehall Foundation and the [[Helen Hay Whitney Foundation]]. She was affiliated with nearby [[Yale University]] during this time.

Wu was a fellow at [[Massachusetts General Hospital]] in the Department of Molecular Biology from 1987 to 1991. She moved to Harvard Medical School's main campus as an assistant professor in the Department of Anatomy and Cellular Biology and then joined the Department of Genetics, also at Harvard Medical School, in 1993. In 2005, she left the Department of Genetics to become a professor of pediatrics in the Division of Molecular Medicine at the [[Boston Children's Hospital]]. She returned to the Department of Genetics at Harvard Medical School as a full professor in 2007.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://genetics.med.harvard.edu/faculty.htm#C | title= Harvard Medical School Genetics Faculty | access-date=25 May 2013}}</ref><ref name=staff>{{cite web | title= Personal Genetics Education Project staff | url=http://www.pged.org/staff/ | access-date=31 Oct 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.homologyeffects.org | title= Wu Lab, Department of Genetics, Harvard Medical School, home page | access-date=29 Dec 2013 }}</ref>

==Research==
{{expand section|1=further specifics of importance of research findings, from secondary sources|small=no|date=March 2015}}
Since 1980,  Wu's research has focused on the role of chromosome behavior in inheritance and gene activity, with emphasis on the widespread phenomena in which homology between chromosomes plays a role.  She coined the term "homology effects" to highlight these phenomena.<ref name=Lewis /><ref>{{cite book| editor= C-ting Wu | date= March 20, 2002 | pages=564 pages | publisher= Academic Press | isbn=0-12-401366-X | title= Homology Effects}}</ref>  Her studies explore [[transvection (genetics)|transvection]],<ref>{{cite journal | author=Morris JR, Chen J-l, Geyer PK, Wu C-t.  |title=Two modes of transvection: Enhancer action in trans and bypass of a chromatin insulator in cis  | journal=Proc Natl Acad Sci USA |year=1998 | volume=95 |issue=18  |pages=10740–5 | pmid= 9724774 |pmc=27965  | doi=10.1073/pnas.95.18.10740|last2=Chen  |last3=Geyer  |last4=Wu |bibcode=1998PNAS...9510740M |doi-access=free }}</ref>  the zeste gene, chromosome pairing,<ref>{{cite journal | author=Joyce EF, Williams BR, Xie T, Wu C-t. | title=Identification of genes that promote or antagonize somatic homolog pairing using a high-throughput FISH-based screen |journal=PLOS Genetics |year=2012 |volume=8 | issue=5 |article-number=e1002667 | pmid=22589731 | pmc=3349724 | doi=10.1371/journal.pgen.1002667| last2=Williams | last3=Xie | last4=Wu | doi-access=free }}</ref> and [[Polycomb-group proteins|Polycomb-group genes]] and [[chromatin remodeling]].<ref>{{cite journal | author=Emmons RB, Genetti H, Filandrinos S, Lokere J, Wu C-t. |title=Molecular genetic analysis of Suppressor 2 of zeste identifies key functional domains |journal=Genetics |year=2009 |volume=182 |issue=4 |pages=999–1013 | pmid= 19528329 |pmc=2728886 |doi=10.1534/genetics.108.097360|last2=Genetti |last3=Filandrinos |last4=Lokere |last5=Wu }}</ref> She has also characterized the mechanisms of bridging [[promoter (genetics)|promoter]] and [[enhancer (genetics)|enhancer]] elements within and between chromosomes.<ref name=Lee>{{cite journal| title=Enhancer-promoter communication at the yellow gene of Drosophila melanogaster: diverse promoters participate in and regulate trans interactions | author=Lee AM, Wu CT | journal=Genetics |date=December 2006 |volume=174 |issue=4|pages=1867–80 | pmid= 17057235 | pmc=1698615 | doi=10.1534/genetics.106.064121| last2=Wu }}</ref><ref name=Ou>{{cite journal| title=Effects of chromosomal rearrangements on transvection at the yellow gene of Drosophila melanogaster | author=Ou SA, Chang E, Lee S, So K, Wu CT, Morris JR | journal=Genetics |date=October 2009 | volume=183 |issue=2 | pages=483–96 | pmid= 19667134 | pmc=2766311 | doi=10.1534/genetics.109.106559| last2=Chang | last3=Lee | last4=So | last5=Wu | last6=Morris }}</ref>

As stated by nobelist [[Edward B. Lewis|Ed Lewis]], "Operationally, transvection is occurring if the [[phenotype]] of a given genotype can be altered solely by disruption of somatic (or [[meiotic]]) pairing. Such disruption can generally be accomplished by introduction of a heterozygous rearrangement that disrupts pairing in the relevant region but has no position effect of its own on the phenotype"
<ref name=Lewis>{{cite journal |author=Wu CT, Morris JR |title=Transvection and other homology effects |journal=Curr. Opin. Genet. Dev. |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=237–46 |date=April 1999 |pmid=10322135 |doi=10.1016/S0959-437X(99)80035-5 |last2=Morris }}</ref>

She also studies [[ultra-conserved element]]s (UCEs). Her lab has proposed that these highly conserved sequences may play a role in maintaining genome integrity.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Chiang CWK, Derti A, Schwartz D, Chou MF, Hirschhorn JN, Wu C-t. | title=Ultraconserved elements: Analyses of dosage sensitivity, motifs, and boundaries | journal=Genetics | year=2008 |volume=180 | issue=4 | pages=2277–93 | pmid=18957701 | pmc=2600958 | doi=10.1534/genetics.108.096537| last2=Derti | last3=Schwartz | last4=Chou | last5=Hirschhorn | last6=Wu }}</ref>

==Honors and leadership roles==
Wu was one of ten people in the US to receive the [[National Institutes of Health Director's Pioneer Award]] in 2012. She has also received awards for teaching and mentoring at Harvard University and Harvard Medical School.

She has chaired the 2005 Epigenetics Gordon Research Conference,<ref>{{cite web | title=Epigenetics Gordon Research Conference, Holderness, NH; Chairs: Chao-Ting Wu & Judith Bender | date=August 7–12, 2005 | url=http://www.grc.org/programs.aspx?year=2005&program=epigen}}</ref> the 2003 FASEB Conference on Chromatin and Transcription, and the GETed Conferences.<ref>{{cite web | url= http://www.pged.org/geted/ | title= GETed Conference | date= April 26–27, 2013 }}</ref>

==Technology development==

Ting Wu has four patents pending on topics related to biomedical research and health applications "Oligonucleotide Trapping" (2013), "High-Throughput In Situ Hybridization" (2012), "Methods For Sequencing Nucleic Acid Molecules" (2012), and "Oligonucleotide Paints" (2010).<ref>{{cite web | title= Chao-ting Wu Patents and Applications | publisher= Harvard University Office of Technology Development | url=https://www.collectiveip.com/technology-transfer/harvard-university/patents?fin=Chao-Ting+Wu | access-date=3 Nov 2013 }}</ref>

She has been interviewed by the Boston Globe on the topic of inventors.<ref name=invent>{{cite news | publisher=Boston Globe | author= Carolyn Y. Johnson | title= Do inventors get enough respect in science? | url=http://www.boston.com/news/science/blogs/science-in-mind/2013/07/02/inventors-get-enough-respect-science/i7wCB2NWW5Ii98XLoO69nL/blog.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130715075830/http://www.boston.com/news/science/blogs/science-in-mind/2013/07/02/inventors-get-enough-respect-science/i7wCB2NWW5Ii98XLoO69nL/blog.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 15, 2013 |date=2 Jul 2013}}</ref> In the context of TEDx and Google "Solve for X" she has discussed potential opportunities for therapeutics harnessing properties of UCEs.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tedxbeaconstreet.com/google-solve-for-x/ | title=Google Solve For X, TEDxBeaconStreet| date=16 Nov 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite AV media | people = Ting Wu  | date=11 Dec 2013  | url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=34-5rF_xI7c  | access-date = 29 Dec 2013 | location = Brookline, MA | publisher = TEDxTalks |title=Ancient Puzzles, Genomic Canaries, Medical X: Ting Wu at TEDxBeconStreet}}</ref>

==Genetics education==

She has worked with the [[Smithsonian]] and the [[National Museum of Natural History]] as part of the exhibit on "Genome: Unlocking Life's Code" which opened June 14, 2013.<ref name=smithsonian>{{cite journal | journal=Smithsonian Magazine | url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/ideas-innovations/The-Scientist-Comes-to-the-Classroom-213022111.html | title= The Scientist Comes to the Classroom |author=Megan Gambino | date= June 26, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url= http://www.pged.org/genome-unlocking-lifes-code-at-the-smithsonian-ting-wu-and-map-ed/ | title= Genome: Unlocking Life's Code at the Smithsonian – Ting Wu and Map-Ed | author= Dana Waring| date=June 12, 2013}}</ref>

She is founding director of the Personal Genetics Education Project (pgEd; link), which works through schools, online curricula, teacher training, and producers and writers of the television and movie industry through Hollywood, Health & Society <ref>{{cite web | title= Hollywood, Health & Society | access-date=4 Nov 2013 | url= http://hollywoodhealthandsociety.org/ }}</ref> of the [[Norman Lear Center]] and the [[National Academy of Sciences]]' program on [[Science & Entertainment Exchange]].<ref>{{cite web | url= http://www.scienceandentertainmentexchange.org/blog/event-recap-science-speed-dating| title=Science and Entertainment Exchange Event Recap: Science speed dating | date=6 Jan 2014}}</ref> Her work with [[Norman Lear Center|Hollywood Health and Society]] and [[Grey's Anatomy]] brings accurate and engaging information about genetics to a broader audience.<ref>{{cite journal| journal=Boston Magazine | title=The Science Behind Grey's Anatomy. How Harvard's Ting Wu made Dr. Meredith Grey's genetic testing storyline believable. | author=Melissa Malamut | url=http://www.bostonmagazine.com/health/blog/2013/10/03/science-behind-greys-anatomy/ | date=3 Oct 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | journal=Cell | date= 29 Aug 2013 | title= Science on set | volume=154| issue=5 | pages=949–50 | author=Bernstein R | url=http://www.hollywoodhealthandsociety.org/sites/default/files/about-us/press/cell_hhs.pdf | pmid=23993085 | doi=10.1016/j.cell.2013.08.011| s2cid= 2253663 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

[[File:PgEdSymboldoc.jpg|thumbnail|100px| PgEd Logo]]

In bringing genetics directly to high school students across a broad socioeconomic spectrum throughout the US and in workshops with high school and college teachers, she uses empirically engaging topics like [[prenatal diagnosis]] and the biological challenges of [[Mars colonization]].<ref>{{cite web | date=May 24, 2013 | title=Ting visits Capital City Public Charter School in Washington, DC | url=http://www.pged.org/tings-visit-to-capital-city-public-charter-school-in-washington-dc/ | author=pgEd }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | title=Dilemmas of Destiny. Genetic predictors of disease can raise thorny ethical issues. | author=Ann Marie Menting | publisher=Harvard Medicine | url=http://hms.harvard.edu/news/harvard-medicine/dilemmas-destiny | date=October 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Ting Wu |author2=Dana Waring. |name-list-style=amp |year=2009 |journal=Genomics Law Report |title=The next generation ..... is in high school | url = http://www.genomicslawreport.com/index.php/2009/10/20/the-next-generation-is-in-high-school/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |publisher= Harvard Gazette |title= When genetics gets personal |url= http://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2008/09/when-genetics-gets-personal/ |date= September 11, 2008 |author= Alvin Powell}}</ref>

She is featured in the documentary series "Genome: The Future is Now", produced by Marilyn Ness of Necessary Films.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.necessaryfilms.com/genome.html |title= "Genome: The Future is Now", produced by Necessary Films |author= Marilyn Ness |access-date= 3 Nov 2013 }}</ref>
